findings.evidence: The paper defines a threshold of at least 70% ("### Definition of consensus Before launching the survey, the steering committee defined consensus as at least 70% of participants in each nonstudent stakeholder group rating an item as “essential” (i.e., between 7 and 9 "), but no comparison in the code uses 0.7; the code compares at 0.75 (`consensus = if_else(perc_essential >= 0.75, TRUE, FALSE),`). Check which threshold produced the reported results.

The text reports an additional study or analysis: 'A follow-up survey of 46 heads of department in 2023 found that 31 of these 34 items were already taught at their institutions.'. Its head count 46 appears nowhere else in the paper, the phrase 'follow-up survey' is used in no other sentence (the Methods do not describe it), the sentence cites no source, and the code, README and file names in the materials do not contain the number. Look for its data, code, table or supplementary item; if there is none, the analysis cannot be checked from what was released.
findings.question_for_authors: Where are the data, code and methods for the analysis of 46 described here?

findings.evidence: The paper reports a median absolute change ("Of the 47 items included in both Round 1 and Round 2, four went from not reaching consensus to reaching consensus, the median absolute change in the percentage of participants that rated an item as essential was 3.8%, an"), but the code computes mean(abs(...)) (`mean(abs(compare_rounds$perc_essential_compare))*100,`) (and 5 similar line(s)) and never median(abs(...)). The reported statistic may be mislabelled.
findings.question_for_authors: Are the reported values medians or means of the absolute changes?
